# Lichess Chess Game Analytics Report

## Overview

You are tasked with producing a comprehensive analytical report on over 20,000 Lichess chess games. The report — **"Lichess Chess Game Analytics: Patterns of Victory, Openings, and Player Dynamics"** — should give the reader a thorough, data-driven understanding of the factors that influence game outcomes on the platform: color advantage, rating dynamics, opening choices, time controls, and how these dimensions interact.

The target audience is **analysts** — people comfortable with statistics, charts, and detailed breakdowns. The tone should be **analytical, detailed, and data-forward**: lead with numbers, support claims with visualizations, and avoid vague generalizations. Every figure cited must come directly from `data.csv`.

## Key Priorities

- **The "White vs. Black: First-Move Advantage" section is the centerpiece.** Quantify white's edge precisely, break it down by rating bracket and time control, and make it visually compelling. This is the question every chess audience cares about most.
- **Rating Differential Impact** is the most analytically interesting KPI — go beyond a simple correlation number. Show how win probability shifts across different rating gaps, ideally with a binned chart.
- **Opening analysis** should focus on the top 10–15 openings by frequency. Don't try to cover every ECO code — depth over breadth. Highlight any openings where black actually outperforms white.
- Ensure the **Key Findings** section is a tight, actionable synthesis — not a repetition of prior sections. A coach or platform analyst should be able to read just that section and walk away informed.

## Data Integrity

**Absolutely no fabrication.** Every statistic, percentage, and trend must be derived from `data.csv`. If data is missing or ambiguous for a particular analysis, note the limitation rather than inventing numbers.

Deliver the final report as **`/app/output/final_report.html`**. Use clean, professional styling with embedded charts suitable for browser viewing.

Refer to `task_input.json` for the full specification of required sections, KPIs, and analysis dimensions.

1	# Chess Game Dataset (Lichess)
2	
3	## About the Dataset
4	
5	This dataset contains **20,058 chess games** collected from the online chess platform [Lichess.org](https://lichess.org), sourced from the Kaggle dataset `datasnaek/chess`. The data was gathered via the Lichess API by collecting game histories from users belonging to large Lichess teams. Each row represents a single completed chess game with comprehensive metadata including player information, ratings, game outcome, time controls, full move notation, and opening classification.
6	
7	The dataset has **16 columns** and is stored in a single CSV file (`games.csv`).
8	
9	## Column Schema
10	
11	| Column Name | Type | Description |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| `id` | String | Unique game identifier from Lichess |
14	| `rated` | Boolean | Whether the game was rated (`TRUE`) or casual (`FALSE`). Rated games affect player ratings. |
15	| `created_at` | String | Timestamp (Unix epoch in milliseconds) when the game was created/started. Stored as a floating-point number string (e.g., `1.50421E+12`). |
16	| `last_move_at` | String | Timestamp (Unix epoch in milliseconds) when the last move was made. Same format as `created_at`. |
17	| `turns` | Integer | Total number of half-moves (plies) in the game. A turn by white followed by a turn by black counts as 2 turns. |
18	| `victory_status` | String | How the game ended. Known values include: `mate` (checkmate), `resign` (a player resigned), `outoftime` (a player ran out of time), `draw` (game drawn). |
19	| `winner` | String | The winning side: `white`, `black`, or `draw`. |
20	| `increment_code` | String | Time control in the format `base+increment` (e.g., `15+2` means 15 minutes base time with 2 seconds added per move). |
21	| `white_id` | String | Lichess username of the player with the white pieces. |
22	| `white_rating` | Integer | Elo rating of the white player at the time of the game. |
23	| `black_id` | String | Lichess username of the player with the black pieces. |
24	| `black_rating` | Integer | Elo rating of the black player at the time of the game. |
25	| `moves` | String | Full game move sequence in Standard Algebraic Notation (SAN), space-separated. |
26	| `opening_eco` | String | ECO (Encyclopaedia of Chess Openings) code classifying the opening played (e.g., `D10`, `B00`, `C41`). |
27	| `opening_name` | String | Human-readable name of the opening and variation (e.g., "Slav Defense: Exchange Variation"). |
28	| `opening_ply` | Integer | Number of half-moves (plies) that constitute the opening phase of the game. |
29	
30	## Data Quality Notes
31	
32	- **Timestamps**: The `created_at` and `last_move_at` columns are stored as scientific notation strings representing Unix epoch milliseconds. They require conversion for meaningful time-based analysis.
33	- **Winner field**: When the game is a draw, the `winner` column contains the value `draw` rather than being null or empty.
34	- **Moves column**: Contains the full game notation as a single long string. Parsing individual moves requires splitting on spaces.
35	- **Rating range**: Player ratings span a wide range typical of online chess platforms, from beginners (~800) to strong players (~2700).
36	- **Opening names**: Some opening names include multiple levels of variation separated by colons (e.g., "Slav Defense: Exchange Variation"), which may need parsing for grouped analysis.
37	- **No missing values** are expected in the core columns based on the API source, but the `winner` column may contain `draw` entries that should be handled separately from white/black wins in win-rate calculations.
38	
39	## Context
40	
41	Chess is a game of patterns, and this dataset enables analysis of how factors such as player rating, color assignment, opening choice, and time control influence game outcomes. The data is well-suited for exploring the classic "white advantage" hypothesis, rating-based performance modeling, and opening effectiveness analysis.

arguments.prompt:
Analyze the chess games dataset at /app/benchmark/data.csv. The CSV has these columns: id, rated, created_at, last_move_at, turns, victory_status, winner, increment_code, white_id, white_rating, black_id, black_rating, moves, opening_eco, opening_name, opening_ply

Run a Python script (using Bash tool) that computes ALL of the following and prints the results as structured JSON or clearly labeled text:

1. OVERVIEW:
   - Total games
   - Rated vs unrated count and percentage
   - Winner distribution: white wins, black wins, draws (count and %)
   - Victory status distribution: mate, resign, outoftime, draw (count and %)
   - Average turns overall and by victory_status

2. WHITE vs BLACK ADVANTAGE:
   - White win rate (out of all games, out of decisive games only)
   - Black win rate (out of all games, out of decisive games only)
   - Draw rate
   - Win rates by victory_status (e.g., among mates how often white wins)
   - Rating brackets: split games into rating brackets by average rating ((white_rating+black_rating)/2): <1000, 1000-1200, 1200-1400, 1400-1600, 1600-1800, 1800-2000, 2000+. For each bracket: white win rate, black win rate, draw rate, game count
   - Time control categories: classify increment_code into Bullet (<3 min), Blitz (3-10 min), Rapid (10-30 min), Classical (30+ min) by total base time. For each: white win rate, black win rate, draw rate, game count

3. RATING ANALYSIS:
   - White rating distribution: min, max, mean, median, percentiles (10,25,75,90)
   - Black rating distribution: min, max, mean, median, percentiles (10,25,75,90)
   - Rating differential (white_rating - black_rating): mean, std, distribution
   - Bin games by rating differential into: <=-200, -200 to -100, -100 to -50, -50 to 0, 0 to 50, 50 to 100, 100 to 200, >200. For each bin: count, higher-rated player win rate, white win rate
   - Average turns by rating tier (same brackets as above)

4. OPENING ANALYSIS:
   - Top 15 most frequent openings by opening_eco + opening_name
   - For each top opening: game count, white win rate, black win rate, draw rate, avg opening_ply, avg game turns
   - ECO letter distribution (A, B, C, D, E)
   - Any openings where black win rate > white win rate (from top 15)

5. TIME CONTROL:
   - Top 10 most common increment_codes with count
   - For each top 10: victory status distribution, avg turns, white win rate
   - Timeout rate by time control category

Print ALL results clearly with labels. Use pandas for analysis. The script must handle the scientific notation timestamps (just ignore them for analysis purposes).

Write the Python script to /tmp/analyze.py and run it.

Analysts measuring "game quality" by length would see 2000+ games as 42% richer in content than beginner games.

Key Findings and Strategic Takeaways

♟

White's First-Move Advantage Is Statistically Real but Skill-Dependent

Across all 20,058 games, white wins 52.3% of decisive games — a meaningful 4.7pp edge. However, this advantage degrades with player strength. At 2000+ Elo, white leads by only 1.1pp while the draw rate doubles to 8%. Coaches should frame white's advantage not as a guarantee but as a marginal initiative that disappears against skilled defenders. Below 1400 Elo, white's structural edge is most actionable (+7.3pp at 1200–1400).

📊

Rating Differential Overwhelms Color Advantage Above ±100 Points

A 200+ Elo rating gap produces a 78.6% win rate for the stronger player, regardless of color. Below 50 points the outcome is statistically random (50.4%). Platform analysts: ±50 Elo should be the maximum acceptable gap for "fair" matchmaking. Games with 200+ point gaps are effectively decided before move 1 — they inflate win-loss records and harm both player development and platform satisfaction.

📖

9 of the Top 15 Openings Favor Black — a Critical Opening Anomaly

Contrary to classical chess theory, the majority of high-frequency openings in this dataset produce better results for black. The A00 Van't Kruijs (1.e3/1.Nh3) gives black a 27.2pp advantage — suggesting white is routinely playing passive first moves and ceding the initiative. The B30 Old Sicilian (+20.8pp black) and Bowdler Attack (+15.2pp black) follow. White players at this Elo range would benefit from studying principled opening play; passive systems are a liability, not a safety net.

⚔️

Resignation Is the Engine of This Dataset — Checkmate Is the Exception

55.6% of games end by resignation, 31.5% by checkmate, 8.4% by timeout. Resigned games are 18% shorter than mated games (54 vs. 65 turns). This matters for game-length analysis: any "average game" metric is dominated by resigned games. Coaches should note that only 4.5% of games end in drawn positions — this mid-rated pool rarely reaches true endgame theory relevance.

⏱

Increment Dramatically Changes Game Character — Not Just Length

Adding a per-move increment doesn't just prevent timeouts; it reshapes game outcomes. 15+10 produces a 7.8% draw rate vs. 4.0% for 15+0 — nearly double. The 8+0 format's 17.9% timeout rate is the dataset's highest outlier, suggesting that fixed-time-no-increment formats at the 8-minute level create disproportionate time pressure. Platform designers and tournament directors should consider increment-based formats as a draw rate and game quality lever.

📈

Higher-Rated Players Play Longer, Draw More, and Resign Less Per Turn

Average game length increases monotonically from 48 turns (sub-1000) to 68 turns (2000+), a 41% increase. The draw rate rises from 2.2% to 8.0% over the same range. This pattern reflects accumulating defensive skill: strong players extend games, hold worse positions, and convert drawing resources that lower-rated players miss. Analysts measuring "game quality" by length would see 2000+ games as 42% richer in content than beginner games.
